title: Neat, secure wire loops, wraps and coils

say: Neat, secure wire loops, wraps and coils.
This is the video for Module 2 of Advanced Beadwork and Jewellery Making: wire work.
Wire turns beads and stones into pendants, chains, connectors and clasps you make yourself.

panel.heading: Wire turns beads into finished jewellery

say: A loop that is off-centre or slightly open is the most common reason handmade jewellery looks cheap or falls apart.

say: Two things decide how wire behaves. First, gauge, which means thickness. The numbers run backwards. 18 gauge is about 1.0 mm. 20 gauge is about 0.8 mm. 26 gauge is thin, for coiling.
Second, temper, which means hardness. Dead soft wire is for wrapping and weaving. Half hard holds its shape, for ear wires and clasps.
Every bend makes wire harder. Bend the same spot too often and it snaps, so make each bend once.
Step one. Leave about 4 to 5 cm of wire above the bead.

panel.heading: Making a wrapped loop
items: Leave 4 to 5 cm of wire above the bead
Grip 3 mm above the bead and bend 90 degrees
Wrap over round nose pliers to form the loop
Add the next part now, if joining
Wrap the tail 2 or 3 times, coils touching
Trim flush and press the end in

say: Step two. Grip the wire with chain nose pliers about 3 mm above the bead and bend it 90 degrees. That 3 mm gap is where your wraps will sit.

say: Step three. Place round nose pliers at the bend and wrap the wire over the top jaw and down around the bottom jaw to make a loop. Mark a spot on the jaw so every loop is the same size.

say: Step four. If you are joining to another part, slip it on now.

say: Simple loops are quick and can be opened, so they suit earrings. A wrapped loop cannot pull open, so use it for bracelets and necklaces.

panel.rule: Wrapped loops for anything pulled. Simple loops for earrings.

say: To open a jump ring, hold it with two chain nose pliers and twist the ends sideways, one hand away from you, one toward you. Reverse the twist to close it with no gap.

panel.heading: Twist, never pull
left: Hold with two chain nose pliers
right: Pull the ends apart into a C

say: Never pull the ends apart into a C shape. It weakens the ring, and it will never close neatly again.

say: Here is a worked example. Esther in Ibadan is joining 8 mm stone beads with wrapped loops, for a customer whose wrist measures 16 cm.

panel.heading: A linked bead bracelet
items: Finished length: 16 + 2 = 18 cm
Linked section, minus clasp: 16 cm
Test link measured: 1.6 cm
Links needed: 16 ÷ 1.6 = 10

say: She adds 2 cm of ease, so the finished length is 18 cm.

say: The clasp, jump ring and end loop take about 2 cm, so the linked section must be 16 cm.

say: She makes one test link and measures it: 1.6 cm from loop end to loop end.

say: 16 divided by 1.6 gives 10 links. She cuts 10 cm of 22 gauge wire per link, and the bracelet measures 18 cm, just as planned. Always measure one test link before you calculate.

say: Coils use a lot of fine wire, so measure first. For example, Aisha in Kano coiled 50 cm of wire and got 4.5 cm of coil: about 11.1 cm of wire per centimetre.

panel.heading: Coils, spirals and woven wire
items: Make a measured test coil first
Push coils tight with your thumbnail
Make spirals in matching pairs
Figure-of-eight weave: count every pass
Kink in fine wire? Unwrap and restart

say: Keep the thin wire at a right angle to the core, and push the coils together every few turns so no gaps show.

panel.heading: Coils, spirals and woven wire

Figure-of-eight weave: count every pass

say: For flat spirals, let your thumb do the bending, not the pliers. For earrings, make both spirals before anything else.

say: In woven wire, the thin wire goes over the top frame wire, down between, around the bottom wire and back up. Count the passes so both sides match.

say: The common mistake is straightening a kink again and again. It will snap later in the customer's hands. Unwrap back to before the kink and continue with a new piece.

say: Before any piece leaves your bench, check it. Wear safety glasses whenever you cut.
Run a stocking over the piece. If it catches, a sharp end is sticking out, so tuck it or file it.
Press a wrapped stone from front and back. If it clicks or moves, tighten the frame. And check every loop is closed.

panel.heading: Safety and quality checks
items: Safety glasses on when cutting wire
Stocking test: no fabric catching
Press the stone: no click, no movement
Every loop centred and closed
